transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Lately I keep forgetting everyday things I’m supposed to do, like taking my pills or bringing what I need to church events, even when I write them down. It’s been very frustrating and a bit embarrassing for me, as I've always tried to be someone people can rely on.
Have you noticed these memory lapses primarily when you feel particularly anxious or low in mood, or are they occurring even when you are feeling relatively calm and stable?

I haven't really noticed a connection to my mood, to be honest. These forgetful moments seem to happen during my normal, everyday routine, regardless of how I'm feeling. Even when I'm feeling completely calm and stable, I still find myself slipping up.
Over what period of time have you noticed these memory issues getting worse, and have you experienced any other changes, such as difficulties with language or finding your way around familiar places?

These difficulties with keeping track of my everyday responsibilities have been steadily getting in the way for almost two years now, ever since my retirement and my husband's passing made my days much more unstructured. I haven't had any trouble with my language or finding my way around familiar places, though; it's really just been these issues with managing my tasks.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to perform complex tasks, such as managing your finances, using household appliances, or following a recipe, over these past two years?

No, I haven't really noticed any major problems with managing my finances, using my appliances, or following recipes. My main struggles are really just with keeping track of my schedule, forgetting daily tasks, or leaving projects half-finished.

Has this decline in your ability to keep track of daily tasks significantly interfered with your independence in your daily life, or are you still able to manage your household and personal care without assistance?

I am still able to live independently and manage my household, like doing chores and working in the garden. However, my forgetfulness with daily things like taking my vitamins has really impacted how others view my reliability. My daughter now double-checks my plans with the grandkids, and my volunteer groups have stopped relying on me for important tasks.
Have you noticed any changes in your personality, such as becoming more impulsive, or any physical symptoms like stiffness, tremors, or changes in your walking pattern?

No, I haven't noticed any physical changes like stiffness, shaking, or trouble walking, and my personality hasn't really changed either. Although, if I'm being honest, I've always struggled a bit with feeling restless or impatient, even since I was younger.
Looking back at your childhood or early adulthood, did you frequently struggle with being easily distracted, restless, or having difficulty staying focused on tasks even before these recent changes?

Yes, looking back, these kinds of issues actually go back to my childhood. Even in grade school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright but "daydreamed too much" and forgot to turn in homework I'd actually completed. I also talked out of turn so much that they had to move my seat more than once.
Did these difficulties with focus and organization persist consistently throughout your adult life, or were there long periods where you were able to manage these tasks without significant struggle?

For most of my adult life, I actually managed quite well and had a reputation for being very reliable because my life had a lot of structure when I was working as a senior center coordinator and my husband was alive. It really only became a significant struggle over the last two years after my husband passed and I retired. Since then, my days have been much more unstructured, which has made keeping track of everything so much harder.
Did you ever seek professional help or receive a diagnosis for these struggles with focus and restlessness during your school years or earlier adulthood?

No, I never sought professional help or received any kind of diagnosis when I was younger. Back in school, my struggles were just seen as report card comments about daydreaming or talking too much, so it was never looked into. It wasn't until my primary care doctor recently suggested this evaluation that I ever considered seeking professional help for it.

opening_question.question: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a lifelong pattern of inattentive and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms (daydreaming, forgetting homework, talking out of turn, restlessness) dating back to childhood. While symptoms were masked by external structure during her career, the recent loss of that structure has unmasked persistent ADHD symptoms that cause functional impairment in her social and volunteer life.
